voice.tone: Direct and explanatory — confident about what the product does, careful and almost legalistic about what it does not claim, no hype adjectives.
voice.rhythm: Mixes short declarative openers with long, clause-stacked sentences that unpack a process step by step; uses em dashes and colons to add a qualifying clause rather than starting a new sentence; paragraphs build one continuous thought rather than bullet-like fragments.
voice.person: Writes as the product in third person/imperative ('MarketingOS reads...', 'You point it at...') rather than as 'I' or a named human; no personal signature.
exemplars: **Email campaigns without hiring a copywriter.** You point it at your website, upload a PDF or a screenshot, and ask for what you need in your own words:

MarketingOS reads your material into a set of facts it is allowed to claim, decides what the campaign says and in what order, writes each email, has every draft read by someone who knows nothing about your product, rewrites what did not land, and hands you finished reviewed email text you can copy and paste after checking the facts, links and brand voice.

And it reads the demand: who would actually buy this, which is not the same question as who the company says it sells to. A company's own material can only ever return the audience it already believes in — it was written by people who have been staring at their own product for years, and it names the customer they set out to have.
Each one comes back with an estimated hit rate and the reasoning behind it, and any of them can be handed to a campaign as the person every draft is written to and graded by.
The current pilot asks existing invited users to test one real offer and share the phrases they would keep or rewrite, plus factual errors and time spent editing.

segments.name: An invited pilot user with a live account who still has not pushed one real offer through it
segments.situation: They did not sign up for this; the founder provisioned the account, and public registration is closed, so they are here because someone put them here and asked them to try it. The account opens into a workspace with nothing in it — no campaign is waiting, no draft, no report — so the first move is entirely theirs: register the brand, point it at the website or paste the real material, then ask for an email. The pilot has asked them for something specific in return: run one real offer, come back with the phrases they would keep or rewrite, the factual errors, and the time spent editing. What is not established is whether they have made the time. A generation takes several minutes, can finish with partial delivery or come back asking for more material, and whatever arrives still has to be read against their own facts, links and voice before any of it is usable. Where they most plausibly stall — this is inference, not observation — is the material step: a website that undersells the offer, a pitch PDF nobody has opened since the last launch, and the private suspicion that feeding a tool a thin version of the company will produce a thin version of the copy. Logging in is free and costs them nothing; the cost is the half hour of honest input and the willingness to read a critique of words they would have written differently.

segments.name: A founder of a small SaaS whose onboarding emails are still the three they wrote in a hurry at launch, and who will not hire a copywriter to fix them
segments.situation: The product works and people sign up. What happens after signup is a welcome email, something about setting up an integration, and a third one that was never finished — written at launch, in a hurry, by them. They are the marketing department: the positioning, the landing page, the sequence, all of it between support tickets and shipping. A dedicated copywriter is not on the table for this particular job; the thing they want is email campaigns without hiring one, and the request they would actually type is the plain version — create a five-email onboarding campaign for my SaaS — not a brief, not a creative questionnaire. The raw material for that campaign exists but is scattered: a website, a pitch PDF, screenshots of the product, a changelog. None of it is organised and nobody has ever written down which claims are safe to make. The likely rest of their week, though this is inference rather than something observed, is that the sequence has been on the list for months and keeps losing to whatever is more urgent, and that the two things they have already tried — a blank document on a quiet evening, and a template that did not sound like them — both ended with the old emails still live. What they are allergic to is generic: copy that is true about their product and interchangeable with every other product in the category.

segments.name: A founder-led seller who writes to prospects one at a time and starts every message from a blank box
segments.situation: Their pipeline is built by hand. They find a person, read enough of their company to sound informed, and write one message — then do it again, and the opening paragraph is rebuilt from scratch each time because the last one was tuned to a different company. Two things make this grind: deciding who is even worth the effort, and knowing nothing about whether the way in they found is real. A guessed email address looks exactly like a correct one until it bounces, and an invented contact at the wrong organisation costs them the only shot they had. They have probably tried the obvious alternatives — a sequencer with a merge field, a list bought or scraped, an agency pitch — and the outcomes they would describe, though none of this is documented here, are volume without replies and messages they would be embarrassed to have signed. They are not asking for automation; they are asking for the thinking that precedes a message, and then one message. Everything after that they will still do by hand, because they are the one with the account and the relationship.
segments.job_to_be_done: Spend their outbound hours on people who could plausibly say yes, and open each conversation with something specific enough that the recipient can tell it was not sent to four hundred others.
segments.trigger: A quarter that starts with an empty pipeline, a lost client that has to be replaced, or a new market they have decided to enter and know nobody in.

They cannot tell which of the people they could write to are worth the hour, so the prioritisation happens on instinct and gets rationalised afterwards.
A contact detail that was guessed rather than found is indistinguishable from a real one until the message fails, and by then the attempt is spent.
The audience they would list from their own beliefs about the market is the audience their own materials already describe, which is not the same set as the people who would actually buy.

objections.objection: I cannot actually get this even if I want it — registration is closed, there is no published price, and nothing tells me what it will cost me once the pilot ends.
objections.answer: Nothing in the evidence answers this. Public registration is closed, accounts exist only because the founder provisioned them, and no subscription price, discount, free-signup promise or future pricing is established. For anyone not already invited there is no documented route in and no honest basis for a cost claim, so this objection cannot be beaten with what we currently know — the only reader we can write a working ask to is one who already has a login.

objections.objection: An AI telling me another AI's email is good proves nothing. Nobody has measured whether a human opens it.
objections.answer: The evidence does not dispute this and must not pretend otherwise: the cold reader is an AI simulation that has not seen the brief, not a human reviewer, and its assessments are explicitly not measured customer opens, clicks or sales; the application guarantees no opens, clicks, revenue or conversions. What it can put in front of the reader instead is the actual reading, in specifics — what the simulated reader understood, where they stopped, their biggest doubt and what they suggest changing — on an execution page alongside the draft, so a human can judge the critique on its merits rather than take a score on faith. The answer is disclosure and a readable diagnosis, never an implied result.

objections.objection: It will invent something about my product, and I am the one whose name is on the email when a customer reads a false claim.
objections.answer: The evidence answers this with inspectability rather than a promise. Material is read into a set of facts it is allowed to claim; the Knowledge page exposes those compiled facts with the supporting source quotations, evidence identifiers, strength labels and the gaps where information is missing; and once a draft exists its claims can be compared against both the compiled knowledge and the original source material. The honest framing is that every sentence is traceable to something they supplied and that they are still required to check facts, links and brand voice before anything leaves the tool — checkable, not guaranteed.

objections.objection: If I still have to verify every fact and link, fix the voice and paste it into my own sender, I have not removed the work — I have just moved it, and I have no idea whether it is less.
objections.answer: Partially answered, and the unanswered part has to be conceded. No hands-on setup time has been measured and no time saving is established, so no claim about hours saved can be made at all. What is established: the output arrives as subject, preview, body and call to action with text export and HTML preview, each claim is traceable to its source on the Knowledge page, the draft comes with a reader report naming where it failed, and incomplete runs retain their delivery count and the reason they need attention — so the checking is scoped and directed rather than a blank re-read. The only credible invitation is to measure the editing time on one real offer themselves, which is exactly what the pilot asks for.

objections.objection: We already have someone who writes our emails — or I write them myself, and the voice is the entire point.
objections.answer: The evidence concedes the ground this objection stands on: the application drafts content only, users review and transfer it into their own sending tool, and it does not send or publish anything. What it hands over is reviewed draft text to accept, rewrite or discard — and the pilot itself asks which phrases they would keep and which they would rewrite, which assumes the final voice stays theirs. The position to argue is first draft plus an outside reading, not replacement of the writer.

objections.objection: Nobody has vouched for this. No testimonials, no numbers, no one I know uses it.
objections.answer: Nothing in the evidence answers this. No customer testimonial and no commercial performance result is established for the product, and the product observations that do exist are explicitly product-capability evidence, not independent customer proof. There is no social proof to deploy, and manufacturing the impression of it would be the one thing that destroys the only asset here, which is candour about what has and has not been measured.

objections.objection: This was clearly built for SaaS. My business is e-commerce — or services — and the copy will come out sounding like software marketing.
objections.answer: Half answerable. E-commerce products, SaaS and other offers are supported as inputs, and the input can be a website, a PDF, a screenshot or pasted text, with competitor and audience research run on the same material — but quality for every sector has explicitly not been established, so fit cannot be claimed. The only honest move is to say so and invite them to test one real offer and report where the output sounded wrong for their sector.

objections.objection: I could get five onboarding emails out of a chat model in an afternoon for nothing.
objections.answer: The evidence answers on process, not on prose quality, and should not overreach. What a prompt does not have: a fixed set of facts the writer is allowed to claim, compiled from their material with source quotations and strength labels; a cold read of every draft by a reader that has not seen the brief, with the rewrite that follows; an inspectable report of what that reader understood and where they stopped; a demand pass asking who would actually buy rather than who the company says it sells to; and an audience segment with an estimated hit rate that each draft is written to and graded against. Whether that is worth more than an afternoon of prompting is unproven — but it is a difference in method that can be shown rather than asserted.

objections.objection: A run takes several minutes and might come back incomplete. I am not building a deadline around something that may hand me half a campaign.
objections.answer: Answered by being upfront rather than by a fix. A generation can take several minutes and may finish with partial delivery or need additional material; when that happens the run keeps its delivery count and states the reason it needs attention, so the failure is visible and resumable rather than silent. Nothing in the evidence promises a faster or guaranteed-complete run, so no such promise can be made.

objections.objection: Handing over my website, documents and real offer to find out whether the output is usable is a bigger commitment than I want to make for a maybe.
objections.answer: Weakly answered. The inputs required are material they already publish or already have — a website, a PDF, a screenshot or pasted text — and the ask in the pilot is one real offer, not the whole company. Beyond that, nothing in the evidence establishes how their material is stored, retained or protected, so any reassurance on that point would be invented and must not be given.

gaps.question: What does it cost, and is there a free trial or free tier?

gaps.impact: the copy can describe the product but cannot prove anyone uses it
gaps.question: Which customers or quotes may we name?

gaps.question: What measurable result do customers get, and how do you know?
